speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the past year, there have been significant developments in Singapore's legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has been made possible by the Ministry of Law (MinLaw), which has made it a priority to ensure that we have kept up with international developments and have actively sought new opportunities for the growth of our legal sector.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the establishment of these new platforms and further enhancements in the pipeline, Singapore will be well-placed to reinforce our "Singapore" legal brand as a global force in the legal and dispute resolution market, especially now that we are able to provide the full spectrum of dispute resolution options.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The establishment of Singapore's third law school is an important milestone in the expansion of our legal sector and will ensure that we will be able to further augment our market for legal services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, there is some concern that the uncertain global economic outlook might dampen growth of our legal sector and would reduce the opportunities available to Singaporean lawyers and law firms to expand further, especially in the region.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, in light of this, what steps is MinLaw considering to ensure the continued growth and development of the Singapore legal sector in general, especially against the backdrop of a slowing economic growth in Singapore and the region?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And very importantly, arising from all of these changes – academic, judicial, policy – how will MinLaw help to ensure that Singapore law stays relevant as the law of choice for disputes, especially in the Singapore Courts or in SIAC, given that Singapore law is growing in jurisprudential depth and quality?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr de Souza, you have your two cuts in two minutes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In recent years, as a consequence of globalisation and the growing interconnectedness between countries, we are seeing a shift towards crime becoming increasingly cross-border in nature.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Crimes are no longer bound by jurisdictional boundaries and are now being perpetrated by individuals or syndicates over the Page: 89 Internet or through other electronic means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, given the increasingly complex nature of cross-border crimes and the need for prompt and accurate justice delivered to the accused person, what further initiatives and reforms does MinLaw envision for the criminal justice system in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Further, there is also the need for a review of our civil justice system, to ensure the continued relevance of Singapore law and our Courts at an international level.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The introduction of the Choice of Court Agreements Bill this past week is one such example.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, as Singapore law continues to grow in jurisprudential depth and geographical reach, how will the Ministry ensure that it is kept relevant to – and at the centre of – any intended reforms to the civil justice system?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The protection of registered designs, like other types of Intellectual Property (IP), aims to encourage innovation and creativity by granting rights owners the exclusive use of their designs for a limited period, in exchange for disclosing and releasing it for public use at the end of the prescribed period.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As part of the Singapore economy, the legal services sector will need to participate in the transformational exercise called upon by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The law practices can tap on some of the generic measures rolled out to support businesses, like tax incentives or business grants.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of the other measures, however, do not appear as relevant and it may not be immediately clear how the law practices will be part of this transformation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One, how local firms, especially the small and medium-sized law practices, can tap on the various benefits rolled out to support businesses; and, two, the emerging trends and developments in the legal services sector and what needs to be done to transform the sector to keep up with the changing economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some support may be needed to cajole the law practitioners, in particular, those in the small and medium-sized firms, to be part of this transformation exercise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is not because lawyers do not think it is important.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality is that these firms face issues of having the capabilities and capacity to spend time in developing their businesses, not to mention transform them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often, lawyers are busy with the actual legal work of meeting clients and going to Court and may not have the expertise or connections to develop their businesses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would, therefore, like to enquire about the Ministry's plans for the legal services sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, what measures are in place to specifically address near-term issues faced by the small- and medium- Page: 90 sized practices so that they can be part of the growing legal services sector?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there is currently a Legal Industry Needs Study being coordinated by The Law Society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What are the Ministry's role and plans following from this study?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Dennis Tan, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that UniSIM will now not offer that course.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that these graduates may have to take the JD course instead.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the JD course may take a much longer time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Past graduates with similar external law degrees who are qualified to practise as Singapore lawyers can probably testify that they did not need such a lengthy course to make them worthy practitioners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, some external law degree holders who have yet been allowed to qualify as lawyers in Singapore are doing well as legal counsel or even practising successfully under a different jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister to update the House on the Government's present position on the prospect of these graduates qualifying as advocates and solicitors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we know, in the past few years, there has been an over-supply of law graduates and a shortage of trainee positions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason why I am asking this question is that, as a practising lawyer myself, I find that many law graduates only choose their area of work after they start training or with their first job after they qualify as lawyers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, many switch areas of work after training or after their initial job.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My next question is: what if, say, a large number of students at UniSIM decide, in the course of studying Community Law subjects or having done attachments at law firms, decide that Community Law – whether Family, Probate or Criminal Law – is not their cup tea?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it realistic to expect people to stay in the field at this early stage of their legal career or education?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How the law schools communicate their expectation of their graduates may have a positive influence on their views towards different areas of practice.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chair, with your permission, may I display some slides on the LED screens, please?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Mr Chair and Members of the House, it has been said by Minister Heng Swee Keat and others that changes are upon us.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: In particular, in this region, which is the Asia Pacific region, we have the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC), we also have the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), which, hopefully, will see fruit very soon.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: We have the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, with which negotiations are also underway.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: I have shown here a Venn diagram of how and where we are placed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: There are about three or four huge international trade and investment agreements.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: And Singapore, as Minister Heng has rightly said, is "at the centre of the Asian growth story".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: If we look at this diagram, we, together with a few other Asian neighbours, are smack in the middle.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: If Singaporeans, businesses and professionals are at the centre, smack in the middle, lawyers, certainly, are no exception.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: As our Chief Justice said earlier this year, "the law is indispensable to business.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Business actors transact in the shadow of the law and they depend on the law and they depend on the legal system to ensure their bargains are enforceable." In January this year, the Minister for Law at the first Legal Convergence Conference, which was organised by the Academy of Law and the Ministry, unveiled an exciting new initiative.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: At this conference, we saw high-level representatives from Australia, China and India join Singapore's top policymakers and members of the judiciary to unveil this initiative or institute.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: My point is that as new initiatives and institutes are unveiled to lead to the convergence, as they say, of Asia's business laws, to give confidence to Asian investors and multinational investors, that are investing both in Asia and in ASEAN, in light of the trade and investment agreements that we are signing on to, they would necessarily look to Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: If we are at the centre, Singaporean lawyers or foreign lawyers based in Singapore will be advising both corporate businesses and advising on disputes and arbitrations.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: In light of this, may I propose a few questions to the Minister and the Ministry, please?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: How can the legal fraternity be supported by MinLaw to advance the goal of industry transformation?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Are there targeted approaches the Ministry has in mind?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: As businesses "build deeper capabilities, develop their people, scale up and internationalise", how can legal services and legal service providers be incentivised to do the same?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: How can our Attorney General's Chambers (AGC), Judiciary, Legal Service Commission (LSC) and other stakeholders be engaged further to entrench a possible industry transformation which sees possibly lawyers providing services to the countries and businesses in the region?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What are the Ministry's plans, if any, to enhance "innovation" in the legal industry?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What might be the possible interactions, for example, between the legal industry and SG-Innovate?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Could the Skills Future opportunities assist the legal profession as well, to "adapt and grow", because "adapt Page: 92 and grow" we must?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What about the smaller law firms and boutique practices?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What are their roles and what are the opportunities for them for continued commercial, corporate and arbitration work?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: If we were to emulate the ICT sector, would the Ministry, the Academy of Law, and other stakeholders consider, perhaps, a "Law Skills Accelerator" or a "Law Laboratory" which is designed specifically for the legal fraternity and what role do the three law schools – SMU, NUS and, most recently, UniSIM – have to play in this?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What are the Ministry's plans, if any, to enhance the current pro bono and CSR efforts that the law firms, the Ministry and the Academy of Law have in mind to give better opportunities for the underserved amongst us to have access to justice?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, many of our fellow Singaporeans do not give much thought in their daily life to legal issues, especially because very few of us have formal legal training.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not something we think about automatically.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, throughout the course of our life, we can easily encounter situations where legal advice and guidance may be needed: (a) an elderly resident, seriously ill, now thinking about writing up a will; (b) a young parent, with a serious disease, wanting to arrange Lasting Power of Attorney, planning for the unthinkable; (c) a fellow Singaporean in legal difficulty; it could be a tort, a contract dispute, a criminal matter.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In particular, I know many professional freelancers who are on a contract for service and they use the Small Claims Tribunal when they are not paid or when their payments are delayed, especially for their work rendered.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A raising of the claims limits will be a boon for claimants and freelance workers alike.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Among all the cases filed, what is the breakdown on the types, that is, how many involved community neighbours, how many are online harassment, how many are sexual harassment and how many are workplace harassment cases?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Page: 93 My third cut is on the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And also what actions, if any, have the Courts or complainants taken when offending parties, after the tribunal order, still continue to perpetrate and breach the order?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chair, Sir, in land-scarce Singapore, land acquisition is necessary for national development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government compensates landowners for the land based on valuations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Since 1998, the ex-gratia scheme recognises the financial and social consequences faced by landowners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When businesses are forced to close or relocate, workers lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are third parties but their livelihoods are most affected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially so when they are older.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Retraining and job placements become significantly more difficult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I note the need to avoid situations where employers pass on responsibilities to the State.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, there are many genuine hardship cases where employers would not and could not undertake.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The payment, especially training support and absentee payroll, could be made via the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will go a long way in helping the workers cope or to seek a new job.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members who spoke.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I deal with the questions, I would like to put some context to it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have a strong reputation for upholding the rule of law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can I ask for the distribution of the first handout from the Clerks, please?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These results reflect the collective hard work put in by the Government, the Courts, the Attorney-General's Chambers and the various agencies in the legal industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must continue to improve our legal system for the good of all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members have touched on some areas where they think we can do more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will cover three areas in my speech: first, what we are doing to try and grow the legal industry; second, how we are helping small- and medium-sized Singapore law practices; and third, how we are trying to improve the civil and criminal justice systems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah will cover the other points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr de Souza and Asst Prof Mahdev asked how we plan to do this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Page: 94 There are always two aspects to issues like these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, on the Government's part, we have to make sure we have a framework that is conducive for the business environment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This includes upholding the rule of law; updating and making sure our laws and legal frameworks are relevant; providing the necessary support or incentives; and, fundamentally, ensuring good governance as a whole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had poor governance, or if we were not successful as a country, then it is a pipe dream to talk about the legal industry growing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at the same time, it is not just the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a part for the Government, but there is also a part for the private sector and the profession.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The profession must ensure that it is in a position to attract and handle high-value work; and be entrepreneurial, competitive and innovative in identifying and capturing opportunities, because they are competing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The legal sector's prospects are, ultimately, dependent on the economy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be impacted by the rate of economic growth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If economic growth slows, then the legal industry, as a support industry, will be affected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But even when the economy slows down, lawyers will have some opportunities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The world's economic centre of gravity is shifting towards Asia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said this very frequently when I was the Minister for Foreign Affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Asst Prof Mahdev mentioned just now, ASEAN is the seventh largest economy in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: International trade flows will increase and international investment will increase.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Establishing AEC to allow a freer movement of goods, services, investments, skilled labour and capital will help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we have agreements like the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) or the proposed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), that can help, too, to increase economic activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, there is also likely to be more work involving regional cross-border debt restructurings, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are well-placed to serve as the lead jurisdiction to manage these sorts of complex work, provided our lawyers are able to do that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given Asia's infrastructure needs, for example, China's One Belt One Road initiative, the amount of legal work in the area of projects and infrastructure will increase.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of creating a framework, we offer the full suite of dispute resolution services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are one of the most preferred seats of arbitration in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SIAC grew because of a very targeted and focused effort by the Government to make sure it is internationally attractive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did away with some archaic rules that held it back.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And later this year, we plan to introduce a Mediation Bill to strengthen our mediation framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also studying, more broadly, other areas of potential growth that may be available to the legal industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Page: 95 Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah and Mr Chaly Mah co-chair a Working Group, under the Committee on the Future Economy, to identify key areas of demand and potential growth, strategies and capabilities to ensure that our law firms remain relevant and how we can increase the export of services and seize the opportunities that are available in the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Working Group has organised discussions with relevant players to seek their views on how we can grow this sector.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev specifically asked what is the role of the legal sector in industry transformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the industry transforms, there will be a lot of work arising from the transformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The new transformation will bring around more work and the legal sector has to be prepared for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will support the universities and make sure that they train their lawyers for these new fields.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked how legal service providers can be incentivised to help in industry transformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, in a way, you are asking me how we can use taxpayers' money to help lawyers make more money through industry transformation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure that is a popular subject.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact is we do also put taxpayers' money to help lawyers in a number of ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we will certainly help in industry transformation, to make sure there are jobs available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will help in the training of lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the Asst Prof knows, but probably in the other university, we helped set up a number of key centres to make Singapore the thought leader in a number of fields and I will talk about that in a short while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With all this help, it is now for the lawyers to go and see how they can take advantage of the situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How can we, you asked, work with the Supreme Court and other institutions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We work very closely to create Singapore as a clear leader in Asia, which we are today, for example, by having the SICC and launching the Asian Business Law Institute with the support of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It only works in Singapore; it is not possible in other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is because the Government works closely with other stakeholders to put these forward and in record time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we look at the whole sector and we work with everyone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Senior Minister of State has written to the law firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can make them available, but people must make use of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the other questions, I will try to touch on them in the context of my speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our lawyers need to step up against the competition and offer greater value to clients, compared to the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will require having stronger overseas knowledge and networks to better serve businesses; building deeper expertise and experience in key practice areas; and forging strong and extensive networks and relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want our law firms to be successful, not just internally, but externally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are actually putting taxpayers' money into it and we focus more of the money on small and medium law firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The big firms, we also have some money on the table through a number of schemes and it is for them to decide whether they will take them up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we do actually put some money to try and get them to make some money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Page: 96 On the promotion of Singapore law, Mr de Souza suggested the promotion of the use of Singapore law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Cross-border transactions, for obvious reasons, tend to be governed by New York or English law, as parties prefer to use these laws because of the law firms involved and because the ultimate end-purchasers of these bonds and other instruments tend to be located around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they tend to be more familiar with New York or English law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there are some signs that Singapore law is becoming more popular.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My Ministry will continue supporting the adoption of Singapore law through education and promotional efforts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We encourage law firms, both local and foreign, to promote Singapore law to their clients.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We work with the agencies to engage companies, the ultimate end-users, on the benefits of adopting Singapore law in their cross-border contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also look at our laws to make sure they are friendly for people to use, in terms of international parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I say strong support, that includes providing money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will, we hope, help to produce a steady pipeline of high-quality legal talent and build a strong faculty and a strong core of practitioners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The aim is for us to play a leading role in developing and shaping laws where we have a strategic interest or comparative advantage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is why these areas were chosen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Specific to small- and medium-sized Singapore law practices, we are aware that they may not be able to compete at this level with the bigger law firms or regional law firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked how we are supporting these law firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because there is too long a list, I do not want to read it out but I will circulate it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Clerks could circulate that to Members, please?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the handout, which will come to you in a minute, the schemes provide support to firms seeking to develop new capabilities, to become more productive and to expand to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SAL and INSEAD recently developed the "Law Firm Leadership Programme" to address the business challenges faced by law firm partners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: UniSIM Law School plans to offer courses that are relevant to family and criminal law practitioners when it is up and running.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also working with the Law Society more specifically to identify how to strengthen our small- and medium-sized law firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will then enable the Ministry to provide support more directly and effectively, for example, how they can access and use technology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We Page: 97 encourage lawyers and law firms to participate in this study actively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr de Souza asked about the reforms to improve the civil and criminal justice systems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the things that we are considering include reviewing the entire framework of legal costs and fee structures to ensure affordability; and enhancing judicial control over litigation, by managing time and costs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Further details will be announced in due course after we have engaged the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the criminal justice system, given how quickly technology has advanced and crimes have evolved, our laws and practices must keep pace.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MinLaw and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) regularly review the criminal laws and practices to ensure that our law enforcement agencies have sufficient powers and, at the same time, we have a fair and robust criminal justice system that is fair to all sides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This review of the criminal law system will be quite extensive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have asked for it to be very extensive and as I have said something earlier in the speech relating to MHA – we will release details when we are a little bit more down the road on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah will take the remaining cuts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for supporting MinLaw's work and for their cuts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan spoke about access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Access to justice is critical to the rule of law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: My Ministry works with the Judiciary, the Law Society and other stakeholders to enhance access to justice, particularly for lower income and vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Legal Aid Bureau provides legal aid and advice on civil matters, such as divorce, estate matters or personal injury.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Applicants must satisfy a means and merits test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Primary Justice Project launched by the State Courts, the Law Society and the Community Justice Centre provides basic legal services at a fixed low cost, with a view to resolving disputes amicably and expediently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since 2015, MinLaw has also provided funding support for the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) run by the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Persons facing capital charges are also ensured legal representation under the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences (LASCO).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The needy can also receive free basic legal advice at legal clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include the Community Legal Clinics network run by the Law Society; the Community Justice Centre at the State Courts; and other legal clinics at Community Centres or run by voluntary welfare Page: 98 organisations, charities and religious organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have been promoting a strong pro bono culture within the legal fraternity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since 2015, Singapore lawyers are required to disclose the number of hours spent in each preceding year on pro bono work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will enable a more holistic appraisal of the pro bono landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MinLaw has put in place affordable and effective mechanisms for resolving community disputes while preserving community bonds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include: CDRT, POHA and the Small Claims Tribunals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The CDRT was established on 1 October 2015, about six months ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It provides an avenue to resolve community disputes, including through Court-ordered mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These typically involve complaints about excessive noise, littering, obstruction or interference with movable property.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Out of 13 claims referred by the CDRT for mediation, four were successfully settled; five are pending mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In total, 11 claims have been disposed of and 21 remain pending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are early results but they are positive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Victims may enforce CDRT orders by applying for Special Directions upon default of the orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As at 31 March 2016, no such applications have been filed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In total, 54 Protection Orders and 45 Expedited Protection Orders were granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This suggests that some disputes are being resolved amicably. 799 Magistrate's Complaints have also been lodged under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if the claim limits of the Small Claims Tribunals would be increased.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is being reviewed by my Ministry and the State Courts as part of the review of the Small Claims Tribunals Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MinLaw will continue to monitor these community justice platforms to ensure efficient and affordable resolution of community disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the implications of the UniSIM Law School (ULS) graduates entering the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The ULS intake will be relatively small – 60 in the first batch and around 75 students in steady state.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will thus not have a significant implication in terms of overall numbers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Moreover, its first batch of students will graduate in or around 2020, by which time, the current situation should have resolved itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, what ULS will do is to provide a steady pipeline of family and criminal lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are areas in which there is an impending shortage if nothing is done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, before I proceed, I would like to seek your indulgence to continue past the 30 seconds remaining to me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Otherwise, MinLaw would not be able to do justice to Mr Dennis Tan's questions, as well as to Mr Desmond Choo's and Mr Patrick Tay's.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fresh graduates from local universities and overseas scheduled universities (OSU) generally choose not to practise in the areas of criminal and family law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a high attrition rate amongst those who do, due to the stresses and emotional Page: 99 demands.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current oversupply thus does not meet this very real need.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The ULS programme, however, is designed to do so and will, in fact, help the smaller law firms who are short of lawyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While the ULS law degree will qualify its graduates for general practice, it is expected that they will practise family and criminal law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Its entire design – from admission and selection criteria and curriculum – is geared to encourage this outcome.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ULS is targeted at mature individuals with relevant work experience who would be better placed to decide at the outset if they want to practise in these areas.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Tan also asked about MinLaw's position on external law degrees and degrees from non-scheduled universities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government's position is that we must have high standards and a high quality of education for the practice of Singapore law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the practice of law has widespread impact – it affects the lives of people, society and the economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the ULS is a specialist law school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Its raison d'etre is actually to produce good family and criminal lawyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The content and curriculum are designed specifically with Singapore law in mind.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not just a matter of converting something that you have learnt overseas.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The content will focus on things like the Women's Charter, Criminal Procedure Code, Penal Code, Misuse of Drugs Act, the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act – all of which are not taught by overseas universities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moreover, it has a unique practice-oriented approach which is embedded in the curriculum.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will have to learn things like the judge-led approach which is part of our family law reforms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When you take all of these together, we felt that the JD programme would be better in terms of producing family and criminal lawyers of high quality.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Although the JD programme will take longer than a conversion course, we felt that it would be better in terms of outcomes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to NUS and SMU, obviously, criminal and family law modules are taught there.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We cannot compel their graduates to take up practice in these areas, but we can and do encourage them to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are pro bono schemes in those universities to expose them to these areas, including, for example, the Innocence Project.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about developments in the designs and intellectual property regimes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IP gives businesses a competitive edge in today's innovation-driven globalised economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The 2013 IP Hub Master Plan aims to develop Singapore as a gateway for businesses to protect and use their innovations world-wide.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have done well in our efforts to achieve this goal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) search and examination unit is the only unit in Southeast Asia appointed as an international searching authority under the World Intellectual Property Organisation's Patent Cooperation Treaty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IPOS also has arrangements with other patent offices, to allow businesses to rely on IPOS' search and examination reports in other countries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, virtual designs, artisanal or handcrafted design items and colours will be protectable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These and other recommendations were positively received in the 2014 and 2015 public consultations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will support the Design 2025 Master Plan in promoting the creative and innovative use of design as a source of growth and productivity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked whether ex gratia support could be provided to workers in deserving circumstances in connection with land acquisition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Like Mr Choo, the Government is sympathetic and will provide assistance to retrenched workers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, it is important not to conflate what are two separate issues: first, compensation for land; and, second, support for retrenched workers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Introducing other elements will distort what is essentially compensation for the market value of the land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This takes the form of: (a) encouraging employers and unions to make provisions in collective agreements for retrenched workers, or, in the case of non-unionised employees, to follow best practices in redundancy situations; (b) helping workers to retrain, re-skill and remain employable through SkillsFuture; (c) providing job-matching assistance through Jobs Bank, e2i and WDA, amongst others; and (d) Budget 2016, which devotes significant attention to how retrenched workers can be helped under the section "Supporting Our People through Change." I also understand the Minister for Manpower will be speaking on how to support retrenched workers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If there are no more clarifications, Mr de Souza, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Chairman, before I withdraw it, I would like to thank the officers of MinLaw for their quiet and instrumental efforts to help ensure the smooth and efficient running of our economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This includes the protection of the status of the rule of law and its high standing in Singapore, which I know, as an advocate in practice, of which I declare my interest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Ministers and their officers cover major initiatives, such as the setting up of SICC, SIAC, SIMC to create Singapore as a major legal hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Access to justice, pro Page: 101 bono at the community level are also under their purview.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Before seeking leave to withdraw my amendment, I would request and encourage MinLaw to promote Singapore law as the choice of law for disputes, given Singapore laws' growing jurisprudential depth and geographic reach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With that, I speak on behalf of the House by thanking the MinLaw officers and I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
